core.title: Give each component exactly one business capability
core.given: A planner artifact declares, describes or references a component (new or existing)
core.when: the planner defines or evaluates that component's responsibility
core.then: Ensure the component has exactly one business capability.
prefer: Pick the single capability from the canonical vocabulary a component name can express — core business: validator (validates business rules and constraints), processor (processes business logic and computations), coordinator (coordinates multiple operations), transformer (transforms data between formats), aggregator (aggregates data from multiple sources); UI/UX: display (displays information to users), collector (collects user input), navigator (manages navigation flow); integration: persister (persists data to storage), fetcher (fetches data from external sources), publisher (publishes events/notifications), subscriber (subscribes to events/notifications).
Compose the component's name from that single capability term and its role, so a reader can map the name to exactly one vocabulary capability.
avoid: Components whose responsibility spans several business capabilities, or that hide the mix behind a generic word.
REQUIRED, not optional: a component name that does not reflect its primary business purpose. Check this separately from the single-capability check; passing one does not pass the other.
REQUIRED, not optional: a component name that does not follow the pattern {business-capability}-{layer-role}. A name that reflects the purpose but breaks the pattern is still non-compliant.
Vague catch-all names with no single business capability.
core.why: One business capability per component keeps responsibilities sharp and makes the component's name a faithful index of what it does, so the graph stays readable and components stay swappable.
evidence: Reviewer reads each component's described responsibility and confirms it maps to exactly one business capability.
Reviewer separately confirms each component's name reflects that primary business purpose.
Reviewer separately confirms each component's name follows {business-capability}-{layer-role} (capability term e.g. from the canonical vocabulary).
verification: No automated detector exists for this rule; compliance is judged by review. Whether a component bundles several capabilities, whether its name reflects its primary business purpose, and whether the name follows the pattern are semantic judgements; a name-shape check for the pattern could be added as a new observer, but the capability meaning would still need judgement.
Treat the single-capability, purpose-reflecting-name and naming-pattern requirements as three independent pass/fail checks; passing one does not pass the others.
The purpose-reflecting-name and naming-pattern requirements are mandatory, not optional.
The capability vocabulary is canonical, but the source does not state it is exhaustive.

values: component name does not reflect its primary business purpose
component name does not follow the {business-capability}-{layer-role} pattern

fires: The planner declares a new component and chooses its responsibility and name.
The planner renames, re-scopes or describes an existing component.

The planner authors or reviews any plan artifact, acceptance artifact or documentation in which a component (new or pre-existing) appears whose responsibility spans several business capabilities, whose name does not reflect its purpose, or whose name does not follow {business-capability}-{layer-role}.
doesNotFire: Planner artifacts that neither declare, describe nor reference any component.
Counting methods on a component (covered by the separate component method-limit rule).

neutralityNotes: This planner-method convention is almost entirely stack-neutral: the obligation, capability vocabulary, naming pattern {business-capability}-{layer-role} and reviewer evidence carry over verbatim, and no exception or condition is dropped or added. What could not be made neutral: (1) the concrete planner-artifact kind names (plan, wagon, wmbt) in activation.facts[1] and fires are stack-specific artifact names, carried as profile data via roles.plan_artifact.kinds, with the core routing on the plan_artifact role plus the neutral acceptance and docs kinds; (2) this rule's finding ids (activation.facts[2]) and the source term id/wording single_capability (verifier_detail[5]), plus the sidecar implementation field (verifier_detail[0]), are realization details kept bunOnly per rule 7; (3) the concrete example and counter-example names (prefer[1], avoid[3], verifier_detail[3], verifier_detail[4]) are not repeated in the core per rule 4, since bun.json is delivered as the worked reference example. The doesNotFire cross-reference to the sibling method-limit convention is phrased generically because sibling rule ids belong to the realization's convention id space. Sidecar metadata fields (audit, splitSuggestion, additions, trace) are not agent-facing items under the numbering scheme and are therefore not classified; the splitSuggestion's two future conventions remain a realization-level plan, and until they exist the purpose-name and naming-pattern obligations stay mandatory in this core exactly as in bun.json.
